items.title: 22-YO Creator Uses His Content Earnings to Help 1000 Families in Flood-Hit Assam
items.blurb: Assam is battling one of its worst flood crises in decades. Millions of people have been forced from their homes. Entire villages have been cut off by rising waters. Roads have disappeared, communication networks have broken down, and reaching those who are stranded has become an enormous challenge. Yet, even in the midst of this devastation, ordinary people are stepping forward to help. Among them is 22-year-old content creator Produnaya Chutia, who has turned his social media earnings into a lifeline for flood-affected families across the state. Reaching villages others couldn't Every day, Produnaya and his team set out in boats to reach villages isolated by floodwaters. But the journey often doesn't end there. In one village, Bhadora, the team arrived to distribute relief supplies , only to discover another settlement hidden even deeper inside that had received no assistance at all. View this post on Instagram A post shared by The Better India (@thebetterindia) When boats can no longer move forward, Produnaya continues on foot, walking for hours through chest-deep water and thick mud. Sometimes, he even swims to reach stranded families waiting for help. With almost no phone network, washed-away roads, limited boats, expensive transport and fuel shortages, every relief trip demands persistence. Still, the team continues to push ahead. Turning content into community support In just 10 days, Produnaya and his volunteers reached more than 16 villages, supporting over 1,000 families with essential supplies including food, drinking water, medicines, school materials and tarpaulins. From food and medicines to school supplies and tarpaulins, the team continues to carry relief to villages isolated by rising waters. For him, this mission is deeply personal. Growing up as the son of a farmer, Produnaya witnessed his parents work tirelessly through financial hardship. He understands what it means to struggle for school fees and necessities, experiences that shaped his commitment to helping others during times of crisis. Today, instead of using his earnings from content creation for himself, he channels them into relief efforts for families trying to recover from the floods. Looking beyond immediate relief While delivering emergency supplies remains the immediate priority, Produnaya hopes to do more than provide short-term support. His long-term dream is to help flood-affected families rebuild their homes and regain a sense of stability after the waters recede. As the waters recede, Produnaya hopes to help families rebuild their homes — proving that compassion can reach even where roads cannot. As Assam continues to navigate this humanitarian crisis, stories like his show how individual action can make a meaningful difference. Every relief package delivered, every remote village reached, and every family supported is a reminder that even in the toughest circumstances, compassion can travel where roads no longer can.

items.title: When Elephants Cross Railway Tracks, ‘Gajraj AI’ Alerts Drivers to Slow Trains in Time
items.blurb: An elephant herd begins its nightly journey across a landscape it has travelled for generations. Then a train rounds the bend. Its headlights catch the elephants on the tracks, leaving the loco pilot only seconds to react. Emergency brakes are applied, but a fully loaded train travelling at speed can take a considerable distance to come to a complete halt. By then, it may already be too late. This is the problem Indian Railways hopes artificial intelligence can help solve: detecting elephants before drivers can see them. India is home to an estimated 22,446 wild elephants, nearly 60% of the world’s wild Asian elephant population. The country also has 150 identified elephant corridors connecting habitats across landscapes increasingly crossed by roads, railway lines and settlements. Railway tracks pose a recurring threat along some of these routes. According to data shared by the Union Government in the Lok Sabha in July 2025, 81 elephants died in train collisions between 2019-20 and 2023-24. Now, an AI-powered system is attempting to give both elephants and train drivers something crucial: time. Listening for elephants before they reach the train Indian Railways has developed an AI-enabled Intrusion Detection System using Distributed Acoustic Sensing, or DAS. The technology uses optical fibre cables running alongside railway tracks and turns them into a vast network of sensors. As elephants walk near the tracks, their movement creates vibrations. DAS picks up these disturbances through the fibre optic cable, while an AI system analyses the signals and identifies patterns associated with elephant movement. When an elephant is detected near a vulnerable stretch, the system generates real-time alerts for loco pilots, station masters and railway control rooms, giving railway teams more time to slow or stop approaching trains. Known as Gajraj Suraksha, the system began with trials in the Northeast. The Gajraj Suraksha technology relies on Distributed Acoustic Sensors (DAS), which detect vibrations travelling through fibre optic cables. Photograph: (Biplab Hazra) By February 2026, it was operational across 141 route kilometres of the Northeast Frontier Railway. Indian Railways had also sanctioned installations across vulnerable stretches in eight railway zones, including areas under Northeast Frontier Railway, East Coast Railway, Southern Railway and South Eastern Railway. Instead of relying on a loco pilot to spot an elephant in the darkness and brake within seconds, the railway can receive an alert while the animal is still approaching the track. When seconds are simply not enough Repeated elephant deaths on railway lines have also drawn attention to the limits of what loco pilots can do. In 2024, the All India Loco Running Staff Association highlighted that a loaded train could require around 1.6 km to halt after emergency braking, depending on operating conditions. The association called for preventive systems such as intrusion detection and wildlife underpasses alongside measures taken by drivers. A collision in Assam in December 2025 illustrated the danger. The Sairang-New Delhi Rajdhani Express struck a herd in Hojai district in the early hours of 20 December. Seven elephants were killed and another was injured. The locomotive and five coaches derailed, although passengers escaped injury. Railway officials said the loco pilot had applied emergency brakes after spotting the herd. The accident occurred outside a designated elephant corridor, demonstrating another challenge: elephants move through landscapes that extend beyond officially mapped crossing points. Tamil Nadu shows what early warning can achieve A stretch of railway line near Coimbatore offers a glimpse of what such early-warning systems can accomplish when technology and people work together. In the Madukkarai Forest Range, the Tamil Nadu Forest Department installed 24 AI-enabled thermal cameras along a vulnerable railway stretch near Puthupathi. The cameras monitor animal movement around the clock. When elephants approach the railway line, alerts reach forest teams and railway officials, who coordinate with station masters and loco pilots. Over roughly two-and-a-half years, the system generated more than 7,100 real-time alerts. Officials say the coordinated response has helped facilitate around 9,481 safe elephant crossings, with zero elephant deaths on that railway stretch during the period. Tamil Nadu has since added AI-enabled drones to expand surveillance beyond the fixed cameras. The lesson from Madukkarai is powerful: detection becomes most effective when an alert is followed by a rapid, coordinated human response. According to data shared by the Union Government in the Lok Sabha in July 2025, 81 elephants died in train collisions between 2019-20 and 2023-24. Photograph: (Biplab Hazra) Building safer railways around elephant movement AI forms one layer of a much larger effort. The Railways and forest authorities have surveyed 127 sensitive railway stretches covering more than 3,450 km. Of these, 77 stretches spanning nearly 1,965 km across 14 states have been prioritised for mitigation measures. A total of 705 interventions have been recommended, including underpasses, overpasses, ramps, level crossings and modifications to bridges. Optical-fibre intrusion detection, seismic sensors and thermal cameras are being deployed alongside these structural measures. Railways has also used speed restrictions, solar-powered lighting, warning signs, vegetation clearance, elephant trackers and honey-bee buzzer devices at vulnerable locations. Government data suggests these combined efforts are beginning to make a difference. Train-hit elephant deaths fell from 26 in 2013 to 12 in 2024, according to the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change. Each death still represents the point where two very different systems of movement collide. Elephants can travel across ranges stretching hundreds or even thousands of square kilometres. Herds learn routes to forests, water and feeding grounds over generations, with experienced matriarchs carrying knowledge of the landscape. Railway lines arrived across many of these landscapes much later. So when an elephant steps onto a railway track, it may be following a route embedded in the herd’s memory long before the rails were laid. Technology such as Gajraj offers infrastructure a chance to recognise that movement sooner. For an approaching train, those extra seconds can mean the difference between a collision and a herd making it safely to the other side. Sources: ‘Indian Railways Deploys AI System to Prevent Elephant-Train Collisions’ : by oecd.ai ‘Assam recorded 82 elephant deaths in train accidents, highest in India’ : by Pranjal Bhuyan Published on 14 June 2026

The fabric lay across her lap as she moved a small blade carefully along its underside, cutting away the fine threads left behind after weaving. “This work may seem small from the outside, but the saree won’t look right if it’s not done properly. Every thread has to be perfect,” she said, her hands moving across the fabric with practised precision. Shaheen, who is in her late forties, was doing katorna , the process of cutting extraneous threads from the reverse of a woven saree. She had learnt the work from her mother-in-law soon after marrying into the family. Years later, it remained part of her everyday routine, fitted around cooking, caregiving and the other work that kept the household running. And as I would discover while moving through the weaving homes of Madanpura in Varanasi, Shaheen's hands were part of a much larger story behind the Banarasi saree. Inside Madanpura’s saree-making homes Madanpura is one of Varanasi's old weaving neighbourhoods, long associated with the making of Banarasi silk sarees and brocades. Its narrow lanes pass between closely built homes. Bikes lean against doorframes, children move between houses, and tea stalls and thread vendors sit alongside the everyday life of the neighbourhood. It was Ramadan when I visited. Sameer, an autorickshaw driver who has lived in these lanes all his life, guided me through the neighbourhood and into its weaving homes. Over the course of my visit, I entered around seven or eight houses and spoke to approximately 10 to 15 women. Many preferred brief conversations and did not want to be photographed, a request I respected. Inside the homes I visited, the loom told only one part of the story. Women sorted silk threads by colour. They wound thread onto bobbins, checked finished fabric for flaws, trimmed loose threads, folded completed sarees and prepared them for delivery. Some of this work happened beside cooking, childcare and other household responsibilities. There was rarely a separate working day with a defined beginning or end. The saree-making simply moved through the home. Who does the work around the loom? The loom is usually the most visible part of Banarasi saree-making. In the households I visited, it was generally operated by a male karigar , or craftsperson, whose skill shaped the weave and motifs of the saree. But the work around that loom involved several other hands. Threads had to be sorted and wound before weaving. Once the saree came off the loom, the finished fabric had to be inspected carefully. Loose or unwanted threads were removed, flaws checked, and the saree folded and prepared for collection. Women in the homes I visited were involved across several of these stages. Their contribution could stretch across the day depending on the work available, the saree being made, domestic responsibilities and the number of family members sharing the tasks. Shaheen's son, who is in his twenties, operated the loom in an adjoining room. “A saree is not one person's work. I do my part at the loom, but before and after that, it's the family. Mostly the women here,” he said. When an order had to be completed, he explained, different members of the household took responsibility for different stages. He worked at the loom while his mother and wife handled thread preparation, inspection and finishing. That division of labour also shaped how the family was paid. How weaving families are paid for a Banarasi saree Shaheen's son explained that orders often reached weaving households through a gaddidar , a contractor or intermediary within the Banarasi saree production chain. The gaddidar arranges or provides the material and order, agrees on the making rate and deadline, and collects the finished saree. The weaving household receives its payment once the work is completed and delivered. In the homes I visited, women's work was treated as part of the household's contribution to the finished saree rather than as a separately calculated job. Their hours spent sorting, winding, inspecting or finishing did not carry an individual piece rate of their own. “Margins have shrunk over the years,” Shaheen's son said. “Machine-made imitations and cheaper alternatives have made it harder to negotiate on price.” The structure made something else apparent inside these homes. A finished saree could represent the labour of several family members, while the payment arrived for the household's completed piece. For women like Shaheen and her daughter-in-law Nazreen, their particular contribution could disappear inside that single transaction. Working around the Ramadan fast During Ramadan, Shaheen adjusted the work around her fast. She preferred heavier tasks, including sorting threads and winding bobbins, during the cooler morning hours. Lighter finishing work could continue through the afternoon. Katorna , inspection and finishing could take several hours depending on how intricate the saree was and how much work remained once it came off the loom. Before iftar , the meal that breaks the day's fast, attention shifted towards the kitchen. After sunset, the neighbourhood became active again. Work resumed in some homes as families ate and the lanes filled with movement. “During the fast, we work slowly. But the work doesn't stop. The hands know what to do, even when the body is still,” Shaheen said. That afternoon, she continued working on a saree that would eventually leave Madanpura for a buyer she would probably never meet. 'They don't know whose hands finished it' In the next room, Shaheen's daughter-in-law, Nazreen, was sorting silk threads by colour. She separated them into small piles, looking closely at differences in shade that could affect the finished weave. Nazreen had studied up to Class 10. She understood the craft she had grown up around and was also aware of how Banarasi sarees were presented and priced once they reached shops and bridal markets. She remembered looking up saree prices after watching a television programme about bridal shopping. “People spend so much on a Banarasi saree. They know all about the design, the silk, the zari . But they don't know whose hands finished it,” she said. Nazreen was unsure whether she wanted to spend her entire life doing the same work. Her uncertainty centred on a simple question: what would the work feel like if her particular skill had a name and a value of its own? “If someone said, ‘This part of the work is yours, and this is what it's worth,' I'd think about it differently,” she said. “Right now, it just gets mixed in with everything else.” In one sentence, she described much of what I had seen inside the weaving homes. The women were working. Their skills were visible in the process. Yet their individual contribution rarely travelled with the saree once it left the house. A GI tag can identify the saree. Can it identify its makers? Near Madanpura's main market, I also met Rashid, a local trader who has bought and sold Banarasi sarees for several decades. Banaras Brocades and Sarees received Geographical Indication registration in 2009, giving the craft formal recognition linked to its geographical origin. That recognition tells a buyer something important about the product and the tradition it comes from. It does not tell them who sorted a particular bundle of thread, inspected the fabric, removed its loose threads or prepared that saree before it left a weaving home. For women such as Shaheen and Nazreen, that is where the gap in recognition sits. The saree carries the name Banarasi. The individual hands involved in making it ready for the market usually remain known only within the household. When a finished saree leaves Madanpura I left Madanpura as the azaan , or call to prayer, rose over the rooftops in the early evening. Shaheen had placed the saree she had worked on through the afternoon on a low shelf. Deep maroon and gold, it caught the last light of the day as it waited to be collected. She had moved to the kitchen. The loom in the adjoining room had stopped. Outside, the lane filled with footsteps, children's voices and the sound of vessels being lifted from stoves. I thought about where that saree might go next. Perhaps to a shop. Perhaps to a bride. Perhaps to an occasion that would stay in someone's photographs for decades. Before any of that, it had passed through this house. Through the loom in the adjoining room. Through Nazreen's piles of carefully sorted thread. And through Shaheen's hands, lifting the fabric towards the light and knowing exactly which tiny thread still needed to be cut before the saree was ready to leave.
